analysis.one_liner: Creates a Medicare-based public health plan anyone could buy, alongside richer subsidies.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2025 with 5 Democratic cosponsors and referred to three House committees; none has acted, and it remains pending.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create 'Medicare Part E,' a government-run health plan that anyone not already on Medicare, Medicaid, or CHIP could buy through the exchanges, and that employers of any size could offer voluntarily. It would also cap out-of-pocket costs for people on traditional Medicare at $6,700 a year starting in 2027, make ACA premium subsidies more generous and permanent, send $30 billion to states to lower premiums and copays, tighten review of insurer rates, require the public plan to cover reproductive services regardless of state bans, and apply Medicare drug-price negotiation to the new plan. It sits in House committees with no action taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Working-age people who buy their own insurance, workers at small businesses, and people on traditional Medicare. The public plan would give them a government-run alternative to private insurers, with a broad network (every Medicare-participating provider is automatically in), no balance billing by participating providers, and payment rates negotiated between Medicare levels and commercial averages. Traditional Medicare beneficiaries get an annual out-of-pocket cap, which that program currently lacks. Exchange shoppers get subsidies pegged to pricier gold-level plans, the removal of the income cap that cut off help above 400% of poverty, richer cost-sharing reductions for lower incomes, and a $30 billion state fund to reduce premiums and out-of-pocket costs. People in states banning abortion coverage would get a plan that covers it anyway.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Self-employed workers, small firms, Medicare beneficiaries

how_it_helps.text: Creates Medicare Part E public health plans available in the individual, small-group, and large-group markets, on the exchanges and voluntarily to employers, with gold-level coverage including all Medicare-covered benefits [S2].
Every provider that participates in Medicare on enactment automatically participates in Part E, and the bill extends Medicare's limits on balance billing to the plan [S2].
Adds an annual out-of-pocket cap for people on traditional Medicare — $6,700 in 2027, adjusted to medical inflation thereafter — which traditional Medicare does not currently have [S2].

Rebases ACA premium subsidies on the second-lowest-cost gold plan rather than silver, permanently removes the 400%-of-poverty income cutoff for subsidies, and deepens cost-sharing reductions for households up to 400% of poverty [S2].

Appropriates $30 billion for fiscal 2026–2028 so each state can run a reinsurance or affordability fund to reduce individual-market premiums and out-of-pocket costs, plus $2 billion in startup funding for the public plans [S2].
Requires the public plan to cover abortion and reproductive services and bars states from prohibiting that coverage [S2].
Strengthens federal and state review of insurer rates — including for grandfathered plans — allowing denial, modification, or rebate of excessive or unjustified rates [S2].
Applies Medicare's drug-price negotiation provisions (part E of title XI of title XI of the Social Security Act, as referenced) and the associated excise tax to drugs covered under Part E plans [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers fund the startup money, the $30 billion affordability fund, and the cost of richer, permanent subsidies; the public plan's own premiums are set to fully cover its claims and administrative costs rather than being funded per enrollee. Private insurers would lose customers to the public plan. Hospitals and doctors would be paid somewhere between Medicare rates and commercial exchange averages — above Medicare, below commercial — and drug manufacturers would face negotiated prices. Employers that don't offer affordable adequate coverage must refer full-time workers to exchange navigators.

drawbacks.text: Part E premiums must fully finance the plan's claims and administrative costs; its price advantage over private plans depends on lower administrative overhead and negotiated rates, so savings for enrollees are not guaranteed on day one [S2].

The negotiated provider rate floor — no lower in the aggregate than Medicare rates, and up to the average paid by exchange insurers — limits how cheap the plan can be, a concession to hospitals and physicians [S2].

The $30 billion reinsurance/affordability fund can pay private health insurers directly for covering high-cost enrollees, and the richer subsidies flow through private exchange plans, entrenching those insurers in the marketplace [S2].

The permanent extension of subsidies to households above 400% of poverty and the gold-plan benchmark substantially increase federal spending with no offset in the bill, raising deficit concerns an honest supporter must acknowledge [S2].
The federal preemption of state laws restricting abortion coverage in the public plan would be one of the bill's most contested provisions [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer-facing provisions are substantial: a genuine public alternative in every market, an out-of-pocket cap for traditional Medicare beneficiaries who currently face unlimited exposure, and bigger subsidies aimed at both the working poor and the middle class. The honest trade-offs are that the public plan's rates are negotiated upward from Medicare to win provider participation, its premiums must be self-financing, and $30 billion of the affordability money can be routed to private insurers as reinsurance — so the bill buys affordability partly by paying the existing industry rather than replacing it. As drafted it has no funding offsets, so its long-term cost is real.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced, and no committee has taken it up since, so it sits in committee while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Jimmy Gomez introduced the Choose Medicare Act in the House on June 11, 2025 [S1].
It was referred the same day to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Workforce committees [S4].
Five House Democrats — Reps. Beyer, Huffman, McIver, Norton, and Gomez — were the bill's original sponsors and cosponsors [S2].
The cosponsor page shows 5 cosponsors, all Democrats, with no additional cosponsors added since introduction [S3].
No committee has reported the bill, and no vote has occurred in either chamber [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost materially because the bill has not moved: private insurers, hospitals, and drug makers keep the current market structure, and the workers and Medicare beneficiaries the bill would help remain as they are.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers and the status quo

for.name: Rep. Jimmy Gomez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Choose Medicare Act and recruited five Democratic cosponsors at introduction

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor is a Democrat and no Republican has signed on; no vote has been held, and the record shows no opposition actor acting on the bill.

industries.note: A government-run Part E plan would compete head-to-head with private insurers for individual, small-group, and large-group customers, and the bill extends community rating and tougher rate review to more of the market. At the same time, $30 billion in reinsurance/affordability money can go directly to insurers, and richer permanent subsidies route more federal dollars through private exchange plans.

All Medicare-participating providers are automatically in the public plan's network, and its payment rates are negotiated to be no lower than Medicare rates and up to commercial exchange averages — above the rates providers get from traditional Medicare. That built-in rate floor also limits how cheap premiums can be for consumers.
The bill applies Medicare's drug-price negotiation machinery and its related excise tax to drugs covered under Part E plans, extending negotiated pricing to the new plan's book of business.

industries.industry: Health insurance brokers and navigator organizations
industries.note: Employers without affordable, adequate coverage must refer full-time employees to exchange navigators at hire, and the bill authorizes unspecified appropriations to expand navigator capacity.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding the House 223–217 and a public-option bill carrying no Republican cosponsors, the realistic path is that it never gets a committee markup or floor vote in this Congress; it is much more likely to expire at the end of the session than to advance, unless control of Congress changes or it is folded into a larger health package.
